title: The sky is the platter
hookLine: the sky is the platter, sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls: creation performs the aarti (Dhanasri M1, ang 13)
carry: you don't light it, you notice it
last: GAGAN MAI THAAL — THE SKY, A PLATTER.

lines: EVERY ITEM, FOUND IN THE WORLD.
cards: Evening at a Hindu temple. The bells start. A priest lifts a brass tray of small flames and moves it in slow circles before the image of the deity.
Incense curls up. Someone waves a fan of white hair. Flowers lie heaped at the front.

People sing, clap, reach toward the flames and draw the warmth back over their eyes. That's an aarti. Sohila's third hymn takes the items on that tray and finds each one, much larger, somewhere in the world.

teach.b: Aarti is the waving of lamps, a way of honoring what is dear by circling light before it. Now walk through the hymn with the tray in mind. The platter: the sky.
The lamps: the sun and the moon.

teach.h: SKY, SUN AND MOON, STARS AS PEARLS.
teach.b: Then: taarika mandal janak moti, the circles of stars are like pearls scattered across it. More items follow, the incense, the fan, the flowers; we'll take those tomorrow. Then the refrain.

teach.h: WHAT A WONDERFUL AARTI THIS IS.
teach.b: In paraphrase: what a wonderful aarti this is, O Destroyer of fear; this is Your aarti. And the unstruck sound, the music no hand plays, sounds like the temple drums. So who is performing the aarti?

Creation itself. In the hymn, the whole universe, every evening, lifts its lamps toward the One. In Sikh practice the hymn itself is sung as the aarti, with no tray and no flames: the sound is the offering.

A few historic gurdwaras also keep an evening ceremony with lamps alongside the singing, and Sikhs differ on that practice. Both share the line's big picture: the offering is already happening, all around, all the time.
You don't light it. You notice it.

how: Sikhs recite this hymn nightly within Kirtan Sohila, and gurdwaras also sing it on its own in the evening as the Aarti, usually without lamps, while a few historic gurdwaras also keep a lamp ceremony.

o: a hymn sung only at weddings and festivals
the incense burned at the end of a prayer
honoring the divine by circling lamps before it

games.q: the universe's aarti tray — tap the pairs.

s: in the hymn, a priest performs the aarti
creation performs it: the sky is the platter and sun and moon the lamps.
aarti means honoring something by circling light before it
lamps are waved in circles before what is honored.
in Sikh practice this hymn is sung as the aarti, without a tray of flames
a few historic gurdwaras also keep a lamp ceremony, and Sikhs differ on it.

games.q: you're at an evening aarti, holding a tray of flames. what does Guru Nanak's hymn point to?
o: a bigger tray with more lamps.
the aarti already being performed by the whole creation.
putting the tray down and going home.
games.why: the sky is the platter, sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls: what a wonderful aarti this is.

practice: Find the sky, through a window or outside: the moon, one star, the orange glow of a city night, or the daytime blue as it is. Picture it as a tray held up in honor, and yourself at the edge of the crowd beneath it.
If you pray, say Waheguru once.

wordCard.voice: Aarti. The offering of circling lamps; in Sohila's third hymn, the aarti the whole creation performs, with the sky as its platter.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: aarti, the offering of lamps; the word the hymn's refrain turns on.

carryVoice: Your line: you don't light it, you notice it. The offering is already going on. Day four hundred twenty-eight.
